## LLM Recipe

### 1.3 Pretraining &amp; Optimization

#### [Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13545>)

This study traces slower low-learning-rate BF16 RL post-training to weight sticking, which persists even when training and rollout log-probabilities match exactly. Stochastically rounding FP32 shadow weights into the BF16 weights used by both backends matches FP16 reward trajectories across the tested math settings, without requiring FP16 loss scaling. It provides a targeted precision-recipe fix, with convergence measured in RL iterations and less reference-policy drift than simply increasing the BF16 learning rate.

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.13545v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. All 8 PDF pages read, including Sections 2-3 and Figures 1-7. Controlled DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B comparisons on MATH-1460 enforce bit-exact backend parity; mantissa-width and learning-rate sweeps support weight sticking as a contributor. Larger experiments use 14B distill models on MATH-1460/DAPO-Math-17k and Qwen3-30B-A3B on MATH-1460, with AIME 2024/2025 mean@32 evaluation. The simplest supported variant draws one stochastic weight realization after each optimizer step and reuses it in all forward passes until the next step, including synchronized rollout generation. The original November 10 receipt date is retained; first announcement is inferred from its original November 11 LG batch and official schedule.

**Limitations:** Convergence speed means iterations to reward/score, not a measured wall-clock speedup. BF16 often catches up on downstream AIME later, so this is not an across-the-board final-quality gain. Parity controls use 64 H100s and other experiments 64 B200s; seed confidence intervals are not reported. TorchInductor observations cover the old vLLM 0.12-0.17 versions tested, not current releases. Frontier agentic/MXFP8 remarks are preliminary. Stochastic rounding is an established technique; this contribution is the controlled RLVR diagnosis/application, not invention of stochastic rounding. No author implementation was verified.

### 1.7 Reinforcement Learning &amp; Reasoning

#### [Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13560>)

A 1,668-run study compares dense GRPO rewards and prompt selection at matched generated tokens and training GPU-hours, showing why per-update wins can disappear once continuation costs are counted. In its Qwen2.5-1.5B MATH setup, the four-continuation reward trails outcome-only GRPO by 14.3 percentage points at equal tokens, while small prompt-selection gains shrink after baseline learning-rate tuning. The protocol is useful for auditing RL recipes, with conclusions limited to the tested small-model math settings and adaptations of dense-reward methods.

The token budget counts continuations and discarded groups; GPU-hours include prompt scoring, generation, credit, updates and weight synchronization but exclude evaluation/logging/checkpointing. Internal preregistration timing rests on filesystem records not independently accessible in the current README-only repository. Prompt-selection benefits are small, absent on four of six models on the main pool, and mostly disappear with longer training or retuned learning rates. These results do not establish that all dense rewards or published process-reward methods fail.

## AI Agent Dev

### 2.1 Agent Architecture &amp; Planning

#### [ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14492>)

ReTrace extracts action conditions and input sources from a standard operating procedure and logged agent reasoning, then compiles them into reusable workflows whose steps are selected by code. This can remove repeated planning calls from stable, high-volume procedures while still allowing model-backed tools; on the authors’ telecom-only evaluation, execution averages 1.3 seconds versus 170 seconds for their agent. The speed–quality tradeoff remains visible: unrepaired task success is 75.8% versus 80.6%, and the recovered conditions are not formally verified.

### 2.3 Context Engineering &amp; Memory

#### [Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14320>)

WikiTrace links each reusable lesson to a diagnostic summary and its unchanged source trajectory, allowing an agent to inspect the evidence before applying questionable advice. Across the authors’ eight configured suites, this improves average performance by 3.2 points over the same insights alone and reduces memory-induced regression from 6.5% to 4.5%, at 17% higher average test-time cost. It provides a practical pattern for auditable experience reuse, while leaving very large memory retrieval and automatic verification of lessons unresolved.

### 2.8 Agent Evaluation &amp; Security

#### [Agent Benchmarks Stop Ranking Before They Run Out of Tasks](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13541>)

Re-scoring released agent runs, this study separates two causes of benchmark saturation: binary rankings that cannot resolve nearby agents and scores that discard improvements beyond a reference solution. It proposes reporting acceptance gates, anchored graded quality and cost separately, helping evaluators measure useful progress when pass rates tie; the benefit depends on tasks with a meaningful quantitative objective.

### 3.2 RL &amp; Rollout Infrastructure

#### [Train High, Ship Low: Efficient LoRA Synchronization for Distributed On-Policy Post-Training](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13306>)

HiLo sends compressed LoRA gradients to rollout workers that retain optimizer state and replay the learner’s updates locally, separating training rank from synchronization payload. This can make bandwidth-constrained on-policy post-training cheaper: the tested GH200 recipes use about 1.6% of full-adapter bytes with modest accuracy differences, and paced cluster links yield up to 2.22× faster updates.

### 3.3 Inference Engines &amp; Serving

#### [SHADOWPREFILL: Keeping Your Next Model Warm for Per-Step Model Routing in Agentic LLM Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13176>)

SHADOWPREFILL uses spare serving capacity to compute context on a model that an agent may switch to next, allowing that model to reuse its own prefix cache when the switch occurs. A simplified 16-H100 prototype reduces switch-call time to first token by 61.9% on average across four tested model pairs at the evaluated load, showing a way to shorten model-switch stalls; the complete SLO-slack controller and host-cache design are evaluated in simulation.
